options.text: Whether the *selection* failures are concentration problems — specific confusable tool clusters — or a diffuse problem across the whole toolset, because deferred loading shrinks context but does not by itself fix two tools whose descriptions are indistinguishable.

Whether the assistant can obtain a sensitive result without loading its tool definition, because deferred tools are still reachable once discovered — so the access decision must not depend on whether a definition happened to be in context.

Whether the team can maintain 240 tool descriptions across six owning teams, because description quality is the documented primary determinant of tool-selection accuracy and it degrades as the catalog grows without an owner.
Whether the model is on the most capable tier, since selection accuracy on a large toolset is primarily a function of model capability rather than of context size.
Whether the six servers can be consolidated into fewer, because a smaller number of tool *sources* is what determines selection quality independently of how many tools each exposes.

questions.explanation: The measurement — a steady decline as tools were **added** — points at the toolset as the cause, so the decision should be driven by what is actually degrading. (A) is the diagnostic that matters: if the 17-point drop is concentrated in a few confusable clusters (two lab tools, three imaging tools), then the fix is to disambiguate those descriptions — and deferral will not help, because a deferred tool that gets discovered is still ambiguous. If the drop is diffuse across the toolset, context dilution is the mechanism and deferred loading is the right instrument. (C) names the structural cause of a diffuse decline: at 240 tools across six teams, description quality depends on an ownership and review process that nobody has, and descriptions — not model tier — are the documented primary determinant of tool-selection accuracy. Both correct answers also point at a process, not a one-off configuration change.

whyWrong.B: This is a real and important property — deferred tools remain reachable once discovered, so deferral must never be treated as an access control — and the exam expects you to know it. It is not one of the two considerations that *inform this decision*, because it does not vary with the choice: under either outcome the correct architecture requires authorisation at the server, so it is a standing constraint rather than an input. A careful architect notes it in the design and stops there.
whyWrong.D: Model tier is the reflex explanation and it is the weakest. The evidence contradicts it: selection accuracy was 91% on essentially the same model and degraded as tools were added, which points at the toolset rather than the model. Anthropic's guidance is that prompt quality and tool descriptions drive selection accuracy, with capability gains a secondary factor — and a larger model would raise cost and latency across every clinical query to address a problem in the tool definitions.
whyWrong.E: This confuses tool *sources* with tool *count*. Six servers versus one does not change how many tools the model must choose among, and consolidation would in practice make it worse — one owner publishing 240 descriptions is less accountable than six owners publishing 40 each. It also discards a real benefit of separate servers: independent credentials, permissions and release cadence.

questions.mindset: When tool-selection accuracy decays as tools are added, find out whether the failure is confusable definitions or context dilution — deferral fixes the second, not the first.

questions.stem: A fintech's operations assistant answers questions against 900 pages of runbooks. The team moved from a monolithic prompt — all runbooks loaded every time — to progressive discovery: three on-demand skills that describe how to find and read the relevant runbook section. Accuracy on the eval set improved slightly and cost per question fell about 40%. Six months later, a new runbook is added and nobody updates the skills. What is the architect's diagnosis?

options.text: The design introduced a discovery-miss risk that the monolithic prompt did not have, and the failure mode is invisible: the assistant simply does not know the new runbook exists. So the index that skills point at needs an owner, a completeness check and a test that a newly added document is reachable.
Cost per question fell 40% and accuracy improved, so the migration succeeded; the new runbook is a content-update issue for the documentation team rather than an architectural problem.
The skills should be rewritten so that each one embeds the full runbook text it needs rather than describing where to find it, so discovery can never fail.
The assistant should ask the user which runbook applies before answering, so that a missing runbook surfaces as a clarifying question rather than a wrong answer.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery trades a context-size problem for a **coverage** problem, and coverage is a property you have to maintain rather than one you get for free. With a monolithic prompt, every runbook was always present, so the only risk was distraction; with skills, a document nobody indexed is simply invisible and the assistant will answer from what it does find, confidently and wrongly. That is why the correct follow-up is organisational: an owner for the index the skills reference, a documented way to register a new document, and an eval case that fails if a recently added runbook is unreachable. The improved accuracy and 40% saving are real and do not remove this risk — they are exactly what you would expect on the cases the eval set already covered.

whyWrong.B: This reads the metrics as proof the design is sound. The metrics were measured on an eval set that reflects the runbooks that existed at the time — so they cannot speak to a document added afterwards. ‘It is a content-update issue‗ locates the failure in the documentation team when the failure is that the architecture depends on an index nobody owns.
whyWrong.C: Embedding full runbook text in each skill converts discovery back into monolith: context grows to the sum of everything again, which is precisely what the migration was for. It also makes each skill a copy that drifts from its source document, so you would now maintain the same content twice — a worse version of the coverage problem.
whyWrong.D: Asking the user which runbook applies is a usable mitigation for high-stakes flows and it does turn a silent miss into a visible one. It is a poor general fix for an internal operations assistant, where users do not know which runbook governs their question — and it taxes the user with the system's bookkeeping. The reliable fix is making the index complete and tested, not asking users to compensate for it.

questions.mindset: Progressive discovery trades context for coverage — so the index it points at needs an owner, a registration path and a test that a new document is reachable.

questions.stem: A customer-facing assistant for a bank's mortgage team serves both advisers (who need the full product suite, including internal margin data) and customers (who need rates and eligibility). The current design loads one prompt containing everything and relies on the model to work out who it is talking to. A proposed redesign would split this into two role-scoped assistants. Which TWO considerations MOST support the redesign? Choose TWO.

options.text: Retrieval would be scoped by role, so internal margin data is never a candidate for a customer answer — removing a class of leak that depends on the model correctly inferring the audience from conversation, which it cannot be relied on to do.

Each role's context gets smaller and more specific, so the customer assistant is not carrying the adviser-only material in every request — cutting tokens and reducing the chance of an irrelevant internal detail surfacing in a customer-facing reply.
The bank could then retire the single assistant and standardise on one design, which simplifies the platform team's support burden.
It would let the customer assistant use a cheaper model tier without any re-testing, since a smaller context makes quality insensitive to model choice.
It removes the need for any authorisation check on the mortgage data, since a customer who reaches the customer assistant can no longer see adviser-only material.

questions.explanation: The two supporting considerations are the **security** one and the **context** one, and both follow from scoping rather than from instructing. (A) is the important one: today the audience is inferred by the model from conversation, which means the *only* thing preventing internal margin data from appearing in a customer answer is the model's judgement about who is talking — and that is exactly the kind of control the exam treats as insufficient. With role-scoped retrieval, adviser-only material is never a candidate. (B) is the quieter win: context shrinks and becomes specific, which cuts cost and reduces the chance of an irrelevant internal detail leaking into a customer reply. Together they mean both exposure and distraction fall, for the same underlying reason.

whyWrong.C: The redesign replaces one assistant with two, so it increases the number of things the platform team supports — it does not standardise on one design. ‘Retire the single assistant’ is true only in the trivial sense that the old combined one goes away, and it is not a consideration that supports the decision; if anything it argues against it, which is the sign it belongs on the wrong side.
whyWrong.D: A smaller context does make a cheaper tier more viable, but it does not remove the need to re-test — quality still depends on the model, and the role-specific eval sets would need to be built and run per tier. The claim that quality becomes insensitive to model choice is simply wrong, and ‘without any re-testing’ is precisely the assertion no architect should let into a design review.
whyWrong.E: This is the governance-skipping answer. Role-scoped retrieval reduces one exposure path; it does not remove the need for authorisation, because the customer assistant still retrieves real customer mortgage data, and a compromised or misconfigured session is still a client. The correct reading is that authorisation moves to the server and becomes narrower — not that it becomes unnecessary.

questions.mindset: Scope retrieval by role rather than instructing the model to behave by role — instruction is not an access boundary.

questions.stem: A university's library assistant must answer questions using a mix of copyrighted books, journal articles, 60 years of internal seminar notes and the library's own catalogue. The legal team says excerpts must be limited and attributed, and that the assistant must not reproduce a chapter. The library wants answers to cite sources so patrons can find the physical item. Which design meets both obligations?

options.text: Answer from retrieved passages with citations to the specific work, page and shelfmark, using Claude's citations feature so each claim is traceable to the passage that supports it; keep retrieval scoped to short passages and instruct the model to summarise and quote briefly rather than reproduce, with a length guard on quoted spans.
Fine-tune on the library's own digitised collection so the model has the content memorised, which removes the need to retrieve or reproduce text at request time.
Cache the full text of each catalogued book as a prompt prefix, so the assistant always has the complete work available and can quote accurately from any part of it.
Restrict the assistant to the library's own seminar notes and catalogue only, and answer all questions about books and articles by directing the patron to a librarian.

questions.explanation: Both obligations point at the same design: **ground the answer in retrieved passages and make the grounding visible**. Citations are the mechanism — attaching the source to the specific supporting span means a patron can find the physical item and an auditor can verify the claim, which is what the library's requirement asks for and what a fair-use position on excerpting depends on. Keeping retrieval to short passages and instructing brief summarisation with a guard on quoted length addresses the reproduction limit directly and auditable. Note the pattern in the distractors: two of them try to solve a copyright problem by getting the content out of the retrieval path entirely, which does not make the rights question go away.

whyWrong.B: This is the answer that sounds most modern and is clearly wrong on the question being asked. Fine-tuning does not remove copyright obligations — it reproduces copyrighted material into a training artefact, which is a larger and less controllable exposure than a quoted passage, and it makes the source of any statement untraceable, which is exactly what the library needs. It also destroys the citation requirement and cannot reflect a collection that acquires new material.
whyWrong.C: Caching the full text as a prompt prefix is a well-intentioned attempt to improve accuracy by giving complete context, and it maximises rather than minimises the copyright exposure — a full copyrighted work shipped on every request, with no passage-level scoping and no attribution attached to any claim. Prompt caching is the right tool for a large stable prefix you are entitled to send repeatedly; entitlement and granularity are the questions here, and neither favours this design.
whyWrong.D: Excluding books and journal articles from the assistant is the maximally cautious position and it is over-exclusion: summarising and citing short passages with attribution is a normal, supportable use, and refusing all of it fails the library's stated goal of helping patrons find and use the collection. Over-caution is a design error — the answer is scoped, attributed retrieval, not none.

questions.mindset: Where use of content is limited, ground answers in short retrieved passages and attach citations to the supporting span — do not try to solve the rights question by removing the source.
